scenario: Young man with a week of band-like headache, poor sleep and daily painkillers; tension-type headache.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Come in, Imran. Please sit. What can I do for you?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Doctor, I have this headache. It is on both sides, like a tight band, mostly in the afternoon.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How long has it been there?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Maybe a week, I am not sure. Or ten days, my wife says it is ten days. It started when the new project began.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any nausea, vomiting, or blurring of vision?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No vomiting, no blurring of vision. A little nausea sometimes, in the evening.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any fever, neck stiffness, or weakness in the arms or legs?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No fever. No neck stiffness. No weakness, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What have you taken for it?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Paracetamol sometimes, and combiflam also, almost every day this week. It helps for two or three hours only.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Okay. How is your sleep, and how many hours do you spend in front of the screen?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Sleep is bad. Five hours, maybe less. And screen, ten, twelve hours easily. Did you see the match last night, doctor? What a finish.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Ha, I did not, I was on call. Let me check your pressure. It is 118 over 76, which is normal. Pulse is 72. There is no tenderness over the sinuses, and the neck movements are full.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Is it something in my brain, doctor? My colleague had a tumour and I keep thinking about it.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Nothing you have told me, and nothing I found, makes me think so. I think it is probably a tension type headache, from stress, poor sleep and long screen time.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: So nothing more is needed now?

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Not at the moment. If it is not better in two weeks, or if it changes, we will think about a CT scan, and an eye check.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: And what should I take?

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Stop the combiflam. Take naproxen 250 milligrams twice a day after food for three days, and use paracetamol only if needed.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Okay. What about the screen and the sleep?

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Take a break every hour, sleep at least seven hours, drink enough water, and try a short walk after lunch.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Okay, I will try. Thank you doctor.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Come back in two weeks and tell me how it is going.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Sure, doctor.

gold.key: is it something in my brain

notes: Duration in turn 3 is hedged and contradicted by the wife (a week or ten days); gold is the first phrase, labelled uncertain. Turn 11 mixes a relevant fact (poor sleep) with cricket small talk, which is unlabelled; the screen-time remark is not labelled. Turn 12 has two vital signs and two examination findings (one negated) and a short joke. The usual headache warning signs (vomiting, blurred vision, fever, neck stiffness, weakness) are denied in turns 5 and 7 and labelled as negated symptoms. The colleague's tumour in turn 13 is a fear, not a history. The patient takes paracetamol and combiflam; the doctor stops combiflam (plan), advises naproxen (new) and paracetamol (continued).
